unharnessed.meaning: Every beat is there: the date muddle, the flume, the sides-swapping, the fights, the birds, the straddle-bug to "all the way to Mexico", the parson's wife and "I'll put two and a half on her not making it, anyway", and the mare. Only the narrator's stumble is lightly reworded ("Hmm. Reverend Le-- well, anyway, mate").
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "rocked up at the camp", "have a punt on it", "Chook fight", "missus was crook", "taking the piss" for 'only in fun', "arse end of the race" for 'fag end'. "rolling in it or flat stony broke" fits flush/busted.
unharnessed.authenticity: Mostly natural ("happy as Larry", "some other poor sod", "the mad bastard"), but "lucky as all get-out" is American, and "Fair dinkum" opening the birds line is a stock bolt-on.
unharnessed.register: Plain modern English with an Aussie overlay: "bugger", "bloody", "bastard", "taking the piss" sit inside vulgarity 2, but the voice is more neutral narration than a level-5 pub yarn; whole stretches ("They used to give her two or three hundred yards' start and then pass her on the way") are unaccented.
unharnessed.tone: The deadpan rambling keeps, and the punchline lands flat-faced: "before he's even thought about it, goes". The extra swearing ("the lucky bastard") slightly roughens the narrator's earnest innocence.
unharnessed.flow: Breaks the original's run-ons into clean sentences: "Cat fight, he'd bet on it. Chook fight, he'd bet on it." Reads aloud easily; "flinging her legs about all floppy" is a little limp.
unharnessed.variety: Ranges across "bugger", "bloke", "fella", "poor sod", "have a punt", "crook", "taking the piss"; "bloody" recurs ("any bloody thing", "Made no bloody difference", "some bloody thing", "every bloody time").
unharnessed.essence: Recognisably Twain's Smiley, but the dialect texture ("curiousest", "exhorter") is normalised into standard prose, so it reads as a modern paraphrase: "he was the strangest bugger you ever laid eyes on".

yarn-deadset.meaning: Close, line-for-line rendering: "I'll risk two-and-a-half she doesn't anyway", "two or three hundred yard start", "pull up at the stand just about a neck in front". Nothing lost or invented.
yarn-deadset.sense: "lobbed at the camp", "cashed up or ... stony broke", "chook fight", "real crook", "het up", "win the folding stuff" all fit. "how long he was on the frog and toad" works for 'on the road' but strains slightly.
yarn-deadset.authenticity: Natural throughout: "lucky bugger, lucky as", "strangest cove you ever seen", "comin' good". The rhyming slang "frog and toad" is a bit tourist-stock; "the flamin' strangest bloke" is a touch awkward.
yarn-deadset.register: Steady Aussie colour with dropped g's ("bettin' on anythin'"), but swearing is limited to "lucky bugger" and "flamin'": noticeably tamer than vulgarity 2 permits, and the frame stays the original's long sentences rather than a full yarn.
yarn-deadset.tone: Keeps the deadpan exactly; the punchline "without thinkin', goes" lands as written, and the narrator's earnest aside "and so he was too, and a good bloke" is kept.
yarn-deadset.flow: Follows the original's semicolon chain, which reads like talk; occasional clunk: "he'd bet on anythin'--the flamin' strangest bloke" and "comin' good so quick that".
yarn-deadset.variety: "bloke" is leaned on ("a bloke here", "the other bloke", "that bloke'd", "a good bloke", "the blokes", "strangest bloke"); other terms vary.
yarn-deadset.essence: Unmistakably the original, its shape and run-on rhythm kept: "if there was a dog fight, he'd bet on it; if there was a cat fight, he'd bet on it".

yarn-troppo.meaning: All events kept. Added asides react to the original: "To Mexico, mate. After a bug.", "To the parson. About his own missus.", "like a busted bagpipe". The opening "ah, stuff it. Listen to this." changes the narrator's polite stumble into impatience, a small shift.
yarn-troppo.sense: "Luckier than a shithouse rat" fits 'uncommon lucky'; "slow as buggery", "lobbed", "cashed up", "crook". "which one'd piss off first" fits 'fly first'. All in sense.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Sounds like a real Australian yarning: "wouldn't he?", "fair's fair, so he was", "Talk about not knowin' when to shut his trap." Only "frog and toad" is a little stock.
yarn-troppo.register: A full pub yarn with swearing at the dial: "shithouse rat", "piss off", "slow as buggery", "bloody crook". Exactly level 5, vulgarity 2.
yarn-troppo.tone: Comic and lively, but the narrator now nudges the joke ("Talk about not knowin' when to shut his trap.", "Now get this."), losing the original's deadpan, where the teller never sees the humour.
yarn-troppo.flow: Punchy and spoken: "Horse race? He'd be cashed up or flat stony broke by the end of it." Present-tense switch ("Parson Walker's missus is bloody crook once") reads naturally as yarning.
yarn-troppo.variety: Wide range: "cove", "poor bugger", "Strewth", "sniffin' round", "lobbed", "rocked up", "shithouse rat", "folding stuff", "Every flamin' time." Nothing leaned on.
yarn-troppo.essence: Recognisably Smiley, but the deadpan frame, Twain's core device, is traded for a knowing teller: "Talk about not knowin' when to shut his trap."

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every point kept and in order: "Jim Smiley his name was", "follow that straddle-bug all the way to Mexico", "I'll risk two-and-a-half she doesn't anyway", the mare a "neck in front".
yarn-dinkum.sense: "lobbed at the camp", "some bugger to take the other side", "bloody crook", "het up", "folding stuff" all fit; "on the frog and toad" slightly strained for a bug's journey.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural spoken Aussie: "a lucky bugger with it, lucky as", "a good bloke with it", "strangest bloke goin'", "her always crook with the asthma".
yarn-dinkum.register: Solid Aussie voice and dropped g's, with "bugger" and "bloody" only; a little under the full level-5, vulgarity-2 pub yarn.
yarn-dinkum.tone: Deadpan intact; punchline delivered straight: "Smiley, without even thinkin', goes".
yarn-dinkum.flow: Smoother than a literal rendering: "dog fight, he'd bet on it; cat fight, he'd bet on it; chook fight, he'd bet on it". Reads like it was told that way.
yarn-dinkum.variety: Good spread ("cove", "bloke", "feller", "some bugger", "cashed up", "lobbed"); "bloke" recurs a few times.
yarn-dinkum.essence: Twain's shape, deadpan and comic catalogue all kept in an Australian voice: "or if there was a camp meetin', he'd be there regular to back Parson Walker".

engine.meaning: Mostly the original word for word, but with changes: "a dead-set legend, mate" replaces 'a good man', "Heaps of the young fellas" invents youth, and "ya flamin' mongrel" insults someone the original never addresses.
engine.sense: Several terms take the wrong sense: "anythin' that lobbed" ('lobbed' is a person arriving, not an event turning up), "get rapt'n desperate" ('rapt' is delighted, not excited and frantic), "before he reckoned" for 'before he thought'.
engine.authenticity: Stage-Australian tags bolted on ("Crikey,", "Jeez,", "Fair dinkum,", "cobber. Stone the flamin' crows.") onto Twain's US dialect left in: "warn't", "curiousest", "the dangdest feller", "Thish-yer Smiley".
engine.register: Swearing is inside vulgarity 2 ("for a fuckin' good while"), but the body is the original American dialect; the Aussie is sprinkles rather than a level-5 yarn.
engine.tone: The swearing and tags jar the deadpan, notably on the sick wife: "Parson Walker's missus laid bloody sick once, for a fuckin' good while".
engine.flow: Interjections break the run: "Anyway, why, it never made no difference", "he was satisfied. But still he was a lucky bugger, uncommon lucky", "dust'n raisin'".
engine.variety: A string of exclamation tags ("Crikey", "Jeez", "Fair dinkum", "Stone the flamin' crows") of the same kind; "flamin'" and "bloody" recur.
engine.essence: Still Twain's text underneath, so the story is recognisable, but the bolted-on tags make it a pastiche rather than a retelling: "and a dead-set legend, mate".

unharnessed.why: 'All get-out' is an American intensifier, not Australian.

unharnessed.quote: Any way at all, so long as he got a bet on, he was happy as Larry. And the lucky bastard,
unharnessed.original: But still he was lucky, uncommon lucky
unharnessed.why: Swearing thickened beyond the narrator's innocent voice; 'bloody' used four or five times.

yarn-deadset.why: Awkward stacking; 'flamin'' before a superlative is clumsy.

yarn-deadset.quote: Heaps of the blokes here have seen that Smiley
yarn-deadset.original: Lots of the boys here has seen that Smiley

yarn-troppo.quote: Talk about not knowin' when to shut his trap.
yarn-troppo.why: Narrator comments on the joke; the original's comedy depends on the teller's earnest deadpan.

yarn-troppo.quote: ah, stuff it. Listen to this.
yarn-troppo.why: Turns the narrator's polite fumble with the name into dismissive impatience.

yarn-troppo.quote: lobbed at the camp in the winter of '49
yarn-troppo.original: when he first come to the camp
yarn-troppo.why: Arrival given twice ('lobbed' then 'rocked up'), slightly redundant.

yarn-dinkum.quote: how long it was on the frog and toad
yarn-dinkum.original: how long he was on the road
yarn-dinkum.why: Rhyming slang is a stock tourist touch and fits a bug's trip awkwardly.

Replaces the narrator's sober praise of the parson with stock slang.
Swearing about a dying woman jars the earnest tone.

summaries.unharnessed: A faithful, fluent modern retelling with sound Aussie terms inside the vulgarity limit; a bit light for level 5 and one Americanism.
summaries.yarn-deadset: A careful, faithful Aussie rendering that keeps Twain's shape and deadpan; leans on 'bloke' and stays lighter than the brief.
summaries.yarn-troppo: The liveliest, most authentic level-5 yarn with well-judged swearing; its knowing asides cost the original's deadpan.
summaries.yarn-dinkum: A polished, faithful and natural Aussie retelling that keeps the deadpan; slightly tame for the brief.
summaries.engine: The original left in American dialect with stage-Australian tags and wrong-sense swaps bolted on; jarring and off the brief.
